title: React Fundamentals
description: Learn the industry's most popular UI library. Master component-driven architecture, declarative rendering, and state management using Hooks.

lessons.title: Thinking in React
lessons.explanationHtml:
React requires a mental shift from imperative programming (telling the browser EXACTLY how to update the DOM) to declarative programming (describing what the UI SHOULD look like based on the current state).

You build applications by breaking the UI down into isolated, reusable pieces called Components.

Recommended Resource

React Course - Beginner's Tutorial for React 18 (freeCodeCamp)

lessons.title: JSX: JavaScript + XML
lessons.explanationHtml:
JSX looks like HTML, but it's actually JavaScript. It gets compiled into React.createElement() calls under the hood.

Because it's JavaScript, you can embed any JS expression inside curly braces {}. However, you must use className instead of class, and all tags must be explicitly closed (e.g., <br />).

lessons.title: Props & Data Flow
lessons.explanationHtml:
Props (short for properties) are how React components communicate. You pass data from a parent component down to a child component, similar to passing arguments to a function.

Props are read-only. A child component must never modify its own props directly. Data in React strictly flows downwards.

lessons.title: State Management with useState
lessons.explanationHtml:
While props are passed in from above, state is managed internally by the component. When state changes, React automatically re-renders the component to reflect the new data.

The useState hook returns an array with two elements: the current state value, and a function to update it.

lessons.title: Side Effects with useEffect
lessons.explanationHtml:
Components should be pure functions, but sometimes you need to "step outside" of React to fetch data, set up a subscription, or manually manipulate the DOM. These are called side effects.

The useEffect hook takes a function and a dependency array. If the array is empty [], the effect runs exactly once when the component mounts.

lessons.title: Conditional Rendering
lessons.explanationHtml:
You can render different UI elements based on state using standard JavaScript operators like if, the ternary operator ? :, or the logical AND operator &&.

Be careful with &&: if the left side evaluates to the number 0, React will literally render "0" on the screen.

lessons.title: Rendering Lists & Keys
lessons.explanationHtml:
To render an array of data, use the JavaScript .map() function to transform the array of objects into an array of JSX elements.

Every rendered item in a list MUST have a unique key prop (usually an ID from your database). This helps React identify which items have changed, been added, or been removed, drastically improving performance.

lessons.title: Controlled Components (Forms)
lessons.explanationHtml:
In standard HTML, form inputs maintain their own internal state. In React, we usually override this by tying the input's value directly to a piece of React state. These are called "Controlled Components".

This gives you instant access to the form data for validation, submitting, or disabling submit buttons.

title: Next.js Mastery
description: Learn the React framework for production. Master App Router, Server Components, SSR, and API routes.

lessons.title: Why Next.js?
lessons.explanationHtml:
React is a client-side library. When a user visits a React app, they download a massive JavaScript bundle before they see anything on screen. This is bad for SEO and slow on mobile.

Next.js solves this by pre-rendering your pages on the server (Server-Side Rendering or Static Site Generation). It also provides built-in routing, image optimization, and API endpoints.

Recommended Resource

Next.js Full Course - JS Mastery

lessons.title: The App Router
lessons.explanationHtml:
Next.js 13 introduced the App Router. Routing is defined by the file system: every folder inside the app/ directory that contains a page.tsx file becomes a public route.

For example, app/about/page.tsx maps to the /about URL.

lessons.title: React Server Components (RSC)
lessons.explanationHtml:
By default, all components inside the App Router are Server Components. They render entirely on the server and send zero JavaScript to the browser!

This means you can directly query your database securely from inside your component. You only add "use client"; to the top of the file when you need interactivity (like onClick or useState).

lessons.title: Data Fetching & Caching
lessons.explanationHtml:
Next.js extends the native fetch API. You can dictate exactly how caching works on a per-request basis.

By default, fetch requests are cached aggressively (Static). You can opt out by using cache: 'no-store' (Dynamic), or revalidate the cache every X seconds (ISR).

lessons.title: Server Actions
lessons.explanationHtml:
Traditionally, to submit a form, you had to build a separate API endpoint and write frontend fetch logic. Server Actions allow you to call server-side functions directly from your client-side or server-side forms.

This drastically reduces boilerplate and provides excellent progressive enhancement.

lessons.title: Layouts & Nested Routes
lessons.explanationHtml: A layout.tsx file wraps all pages in its directory and any subdirectories. It is perfect for navigation bars and sidebars because it does NOT re-render when the user navigates between pages, preserving state and performance.

lessons.title: Route Handlers (API)
lessons.explanationHtml:
If you need to expose a public API endpoint (e.g., for a mobile app or a webhook), you create a route.ts file.

You export functions named after the HTTP verbs: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE.

lessons.title: Image Optimization
lessons.explanationHtml: Images account for the vast majority of web page weight. The Next.js <Image> component automatically converts images to modern formats like WebP, serves correctly sized images based on the user's device, and lazy-loads them to prevent layout shift.

title: Node.js Backend
description: Learn how to build scalable, high-performance servers using JavaScript runtime.

lessons.title: What is Node.js?
lessons.explanationHtml:
Node.js is not a framework or a language. It is a C++ program built on top of Google Chrome's V8 JavaScript engine that allows you to run JavaScript code outside of a web browser.

Because it uses an event-driven, non-blocking I/O model, Node.js is incredibly efficient for building data-intensive real-time applications.

Recommended Resource

Node.js Tutorial for Beginners - Programming with Mosh

lessons.title: The Event Loop
lessons.explanationHtml:
JavaScript is single-threaded. So how can Node.js handle thousands of concurrent requests? The Event Loop.

When Node receives an I/O request (like reading from a database), it offloads that heavy work to the operating system and continues executing other code. When the database finishes, it places a callback in the event queue to be executed. This is why you must NEVER write synchronous, blocking code in Node.

lessons.title: Building Servers with Express
lessons.explanationHtml:
While you can build a server using Node's built-in http module, the Express.js framework makes routing and handling requests vastly simpler.

Express is minimalist, unopinionated, and the industry standard for Node.js REST APIs.

lessons.title: Understanding Middleware
lessons.explanationHtml:
Middleware functions are functions that have access to the request (req) and response (res) objects. They sit in the middle of the request-response cycle.

You use middleware to parse JSON bodies, handle CORS, log requests, or authenticate users before allowing them to hit your route handlers.

lessons.title: Environment Variables (.env)
lessons.explanationHtml:
Never hardcode API keys or database passwords in your source code. If you commit them to GitHub, bots will steal them in seconds.

Use the dotenv package to load secrets from a local .env file into Node's process.env object.

lessons.title: Global Error Handling
lessons.explanationHtml:
If an asynchronous route handler throws an error and you don't catch it, your entire Node server will crash.

In Express, you can define a special middleware function with exactly four arguments (err, req, res, next) to catch and format all errors gracefully.

lessons.title: JWT Authentication
lessons.explanationHtml:
JSON Web Tokens (JWT) are a stateless way to authenticate users. When a user logs in, you generate a signed token and send it back. The user includes this token in the header of subsequent requests.

Because the token is cryptographically signed, you can verify the user's identity without querying the database every time.
